analysis.one_liner: Requires disclosure of big-money political spending, bans member lobbying, and slows the regulator revolving door.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2016 with 31 Senate cosponsors (29 Democrats and 2 independents), it was referred to the Rules Committee and never received a committee or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill bundles several campaign-finance and ethics reforms into one package. It would require corporations, unions, and super PACs that spend more than $10,000 on elections to report the people funding them within 24 hours; treat super PAC spending coordinated with a candidate as an illegal campaign contribution; require campaigns to report any donor who gives $1,000 or more within 48 hours; replace the Federal Election Commission with a five-member Federal Election Administration; ban former Members of Congress from lobbying Congress for life; and bar financial regulators from taking jobs or payments from the firms they used to police.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is paying for the political ads they see; candidates who rely on small donors rather than super PACs; and government watchdogs, since enforcement of election law would move to a stronger, faster agency. Former regulators and agency ethics offices also gain clearer conflict-of-interest rules.

how_it_helps.text: Any corporation, tax-exempt group, labor organization, or super PAC that spends more than $10,000 on campaign-related activity would have to file a report under penalty of perjury, listing every payment over $1,000 and naming donors who gave $10,000 or more.

Spending on ads coordinated with a candidate's campaign would be treated as an illegal contribution to that candidate, with penalties of up to 300% of the over-limit payment, and candidates and federal officeholders would be barred from raising money for super PACs.

Political committees would have to notify the election agency within 48 hours whenever any single contributor's giving reaches $1,000 in a year, and Senate campaigns would file directly with that agency.

The bill would replace the six-member Federal Election Commission, which is split evenly between the parties and often deadlocked, with a five-member Federal Election Administration that can decide by majority vote and enforce the law directly.

Former Members of Congress would face a lifetime ban on lobbying current Members, the lobbyist registration threshold would tighten, and financial regulators would be barred from taking contingent compensation from private employers or working for firms they regulated.

analysis.who_pays: Super PAC operators and tax-exempt groups that currently spend without naming their funders; wealthy donors who would be publicly identified; lobbying firms, which would lose former Members and registered contacts; and financial firms that hire former regulators, who would face new time restrictions on such hiring.
analysis.who_pays_short: Super PACs, big donors, and lobbying firms

drawbacks.text: Expanded disclosure of donors raises a fair objection that it could expose private citizens to harassment, and the bill's broad definition of 'functional equivalent of express advocacy' would likely draw constitutional challenges over political speech.

A lifetime lobbying ban on former Members is far stricter than current revolving-door rules and would permanently bar experienced former lawmakers from advocacy work, a restriction critics call overly broad.
Groups above the $10,000 spending threshold, including smaller advocacy organizations and labor unions as well as corporations, would bear significant new reporting and compliance costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: voters would know who funds campaign advertising within a day of the money moving, and candidates could no longer raise unlimited super PAC money around the edges of the law. The costs are real but weigh lighter: compliance burdens on advocacy groups, a possible Supreme Court fight over the speech definitions, and a lifetime lobbying ban that goes further than most ethics proposals. On balance the bill is designed to shift influence from concentrated money toward voters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled action on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the bill on June 16, 2016, with 25 original cosponsors, nearly all Senate Democrats plus independents Angus King and Bernie Sanders.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration on the day of introduction.
Cosponsorship grew to 31 senators: 29 Democrats and 2 independents, with no Republican support listed.
No further action was taken after the referral: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion action appears in the record before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, super PAC operators and tax-exempt groups kept spending without naming donors, wealthy donors kept their anonymity, lobbying firms kept access to former Members, and financial firms kept unrestricted access to former regulators. No voter-facing disclosure became law in this Congress through this bill.

industries.industry: Super PACs and undisclosed political spenders (corporations and 501(c) 'dark money' groups)
industries.note: The bill would force these groups to report their funders within 24 hours of crossing a $10,000 spending threshold and ban candidate coordination with super PACs, ending the anonymity that makes unlimited spending valuable. Voters gain the identity of the funders behind the ads they see.

Donors giving $10,000 or more to spending groups and $1,000 or more to committees would be publicly named within 48 hours. The benefit to the public is transparency; the cost falls on the largest donors, whose influence partly depends on not being named.

A lifetime ban on former Members lobbying current Members, plus a tightened lobbyist definition (one contact over two years instead of three months of being 20% of time), would shrink the pool of connected former lawmakers and capture more of the industry as registrants.

The bill bars regulators from taking jobs with firms they regulated, blocks contingent 'golden parachute' payments for leaving government, and restricts federal banking examiners from working for the banks they supervised. Firms would lose a hiring pipeline that gives them insider knowledge of their own oversight.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill, so their campaign spending would face the same 24-hour disclosure as corporations'. Unions gain from candidate-coordination rules but bear new reporting costs on top of limits they already follow.

Members and federal officeholders could no longer raise money for super PACs, and former colleagues would be barred from lobbying them for life. The bill restricts officeholders' own future options and their access to outside spending.
